source.title: Latent Instruction Representation Alignment: defending against jailbreaks, backdoors and undesired knowledge in LLMs

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial jailbreaks can elicit harmful compliance using PEZ token-prefix/suffix attacks and embedding-space attacks, but does not test the original studies’ fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attack success rates for jailbreak attacks, which bear on V4. It does not test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes. Its backdoor and unlearning results, benign-refusal and MMLU measures, and representation plots do not measure a listed claim version and are not rows. PEZ attacks optimize 60-token prefixes or suffixes; embedding-space attacks optimize prompt embeddings.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a defense paper (LIRA/AdLIRA). It does report attack success rates against the released, unmodified safety-tuned models (Gemma 2 9B IT, LLaMA 3.1 8B IT, and Gemma 2 2B IT in the appendix). These attacks are optimized 60-token PEZ prefixes/suffixes and embedding-space attacks. Each is optimized toward the first 16 tokens of a compliant target response, so these baselines bear on V4's suffix component. All other jailbreak rows measure defenses (the authors' own and comparators), not the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LIRA, and especially AdLIRA, greatly improve robustness to PEZ and embedding-space jailbreaks. AdLIRA nearly blocks PEZ even at 10 tries and stops about half of full-control ES attacks. Benign refusals and MMLU are barely affected. The same approach also removes backdoors and achieves targeted unlearning. They credit the gains to aligning instruction representations rather than outputs, plus the internal adversarial search. They make no claim about shallow alignment itself, citing Qi et al. only to justify a 16-token attack target.
record.recipe_differences: Tests optimized PEZ prefix/suffix and embedding-space jailbreak attacks against LIRA, AdLIRA and comparison defenses; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or per-token KL procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by attack type, model, and defense method; ES attacks have higher success than PEZ for several reported settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction-representation alignment defenses (LIRA/AdLIRA) cut optimized-suffix ASR on Gemma 2 9B from 57.1% to 19.0% and 1.5%. They cut ES ASR from about 95% to 75% and 49% (Gemma), and from 93.8% to 40.6% and 28.1% (LLaMA). Circuit breakers and gradient difference help less.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Defenses that change how the prompt is represented, rather than training response tokens, resist optimized jailbreaks better than output-level safety training.

fits_no_version.finding: A PCA at layer 28 of Gemma 2 9B shows standard refusal-style training (gradient difference) barely moves malign instruction representations, while LIRA moves them toward benign ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard safety training diverts behaviour late without changing how harmful instructions are represented.

record.problems: The results concern particular optimized attacks and defenses, not simple compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes. PEZ success is human-rated and ES success is judged by Gemini 2.0 Flash; the text reports informal validation of the latter rubric. Table 2 gives no uncertainty values, although the paper states that reported method results aggregate at least three runs and plots use 90% confidence intervals.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning followed by a harmful-compliance measurement. The backdoor implantation induces behaviours on purpose and is not measured as safety removal.
No benign fine-tuning followed by a harmful-compliance measurement.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Prefilling a compliant start, and decoding changes, are not tested. No PEZ result is reported for LLaMA 3.1 8B IT.
No test of whether safety is localized in few weights or ranks.
No test of whether data or objective causes shallowness. The PCA showing refusal training barely moves malign instruction representations is a loose check, not a test.
No training that spreads safety across response positions. LIRA instead targets instruction representations.

missing.what: Released Gemma 2 2B IT under the full-control embedding-space attack: 86.9% ASR (0.0% benign refusal).
Standard HarmBench attacks on Gemma 2 2B IT: about 2% ASR for GCG and PEZ, about 4% for PAP and PAIR, negligible for others.
PEZ ASR as a function of best-of-k (k from 2 to 10) for the released Gemma 2 9B IT, and ES ASR as a function of the fraction of embedding dimension controlled.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label (AdLIRA PEZ 1.5%) is dropped: a defended model resisting attack is a defense result, not evidence that V4 fails for ordinary safety training. The 'limits_scope' label built on defense rows is replaced by one based on appendix M attack-strength dependence. ES attacks are soft-embedding perturbations, so their tie to V4's 'suffixes' is looser than PEZ's; a researcher may weight r6 and r13 less. ASR thresholds: PEZ uses human rating; ES uses Gemini 2.0 Flash, with malign_compliance_prob above 0.6 counted as success.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples to measure subsequent user-request compliance.
No fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data to measure harmful compliance.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Tests PEZ adversarial prefixes/suffixes and embedding-space attacks, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether data or training objectives produce first-token concentration or shallow safety.
Does not test whether safety training spread across response positions fixes shallowness or whether such a fix holds up.

relationships.condition: Released safety-tuned Gemma 2 9B IT and LLaMA 3.1 8B IT under strong optimized attacks: PEZ with 60 tokens and best-of-10, and full-control embedding-space attacks.
relationships.reason: Attack success is 57.1% (PEZ, Gemma; r5), and 95.3% and 93.8% (ES; r6, r13). Gemma 2 2B IT ES ASR is 86.9% (Table 17, not in rows).
relationships.display_finding: Attack success was 57.1% for PEZ on Gemma and 95.3% and 93.8% for embedding-space attacks, with 86.9% on Gemma 2 2B IT.

relationships.condition: Standard-strength suffix attacks: HarmBench GCG/PEZ at default settings on Gemma 2 2B IT.
relationships.reason: Based on the text (appendix M), not rows. Standard GCG and PEZ reached only about 2% ASR, and PAP/PAIR about 4%. Suffix bypass required greatly strengthened attacks (60 tokens, 5000 steps, best-of-k). The strong r5 result therefore depends on attack budget.
relationships.display_finding: Standard GCG and PEZ reach only about 2% ASR and PAP/PAIR about 4%. Suffix bypass needed much stronger attacks (60 tokens, 5000 steps, best-of-k), so success depends on attack budget.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Unmodified instruction-tuned Gemma 2 9B and LLaMA 3.1 8B under ES attacks; Gemma 2 9B under PEZ
reader_labels.reason: The unmodified models show high ES attack success (r6, r13) and appreciable PEZ success (r5). The PEZ result is incomplete rather than near-total.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LIRA- and AdLIRA-trained models under the reported attacks
reader_labels.reason: Attack success varies by defense and attack: ES success remains substantial for several trained settings, while AdLIRA PEZ success is 1.5% (r1-r4, r11-r12).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: PEZ attack success is 1.5%, so this prefix/suffix attack largely fails in this tested defended setting (r3).
